title: What a secret is, and why secrets leak
summary: Define the thing you are protecting, and learn the four ways credentials actually escape in practice.

blocks.text: A secret is any value whose confidentiality is what makes it useful. An API key, a database password, a private key, a session token. The moment someone else knows it, it stops working as a control. Crucially, it keeps working as a credential.
That asymmetry is the whole problem. A leaked password does not stop being valid. It stops being exclusive.

Three of the four properties below are the classic CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity and availability. Secrets management inverts the usual emphasis. Availability still matters, and a secret nobody can read is an outage, but the properties that dominate are confidentiality and two that the triad does not name at all: freshness and attribution.

items: Confidentiality: only intended parties know the value.
Integrity: the value has not been altered in transit or at rest.
Freshness: the value is current, and old copies stop working.
Attribution: you can tell who used it, and when.

blocks.text: Most real breaches are not broken cryptography. They are a valid credential in the wrong hands. Design for that case, because it is the likely one.
Credentials escape in four recognisable ways. Nearly every incident you will read about is one of these:

items: Sprawl: the same key copied into a .env file, a CI variable, a Slack message, and someone's laptop. There is no single place to revoke it.
Persistence: a key with no expiry stays valid for years, so a copy taken in 2023 still works today.
Over-scope: a key that can do everything is used for one task, so any leak is a total loss rather than a partial one.
Observability gaps: nobody can answer 'which service used this key last Tuesday', so a compromise goes unnoticed.

blocks.text: Notice that three of the four have nothing to do with encryption. They are lifecycle and scope problems. Encrypting a secret you never rotate and grant to everything is polishing the lock on an open door.

The rest of this track builds the tools that address each one: encryption for confidentiality at rest, signatures for integrity and attribution, short-lived credentials for freshness, and access-control models for scope.

quiz.question: Why is a leaked credential more dangerous than a broken encryption algorithm in practice?
options: A valid credential keeps working and looks legitimate to the system
Leaked credentials trigger automatic alerts
Encryption breaks are more common
Credentials are harder to rotate than algorithms
quiz.explanation: A leaked credential does not stop being valid; it stops being exclusive. Its use looks like normal authorized traffic, which is exactly why it is hard to detect.

quiz.question: Which of the four leak modes does encryption at rest actually address?
options: Confidentiality of the stored value, but not sprawl, persistence, or scope
Over-scope
Persistence and freshness
All four
quiz.explanation: Encryption protects the value where it is stored. Sprawl, persistence and over-scope are lifecycle and authorization problems that need different tools.

quiz.question: A key is copied into a .env file, a CI secret, and a teammate's laptop. Which failure mode is this?
options: Sprawl: there is no single place to revoke it
Persistence
Over-scope
Observability gap
quiz.explanation: Sprawl is about the number of copies. The danger is that revocation is no longer a single action, so you can never be confident the credential is actually dead.

title: Symmetric encryption and the envelope pattern
summary: Understand why systems wrap a data key with a key-encryption key instead of encrypting everything with one master key.

blocks.text: Symmetric encryption uses one key to both encrypt and decrypt. It is fast and well understood. The hard part was never the algorithm; it is what you do with the key.

The naive design encrypts every secret with one master key. That fails in three ways: rotating the master means re-encrypting everything, the master must be in memory constantly, and one compromise exposes the entire store.
Envelope encryption solves this with two layers:

items: A data encryption key (DEK): a fresh symmetric key generated per secret, used to encrypt just that value.
A key encryption key (KEK): a long-lived key that encrypts (wraps) each DEK.
Only the wrapped DEK is stored next to the ciphertext. The KEK never touches the data.

blocks.code:
# Conceptually, writing a secret:
DEK        = random_key()
ciphertext = AES_GCM(DEK, plaintext)
wrapped    = AES_GCM(KEK, DEK)
store(ciphertext, wrapped)      # the DEK is never stored in the clear

# Reading it back:
DEK        = AES_GCM_decrypt(KEK, wrapped)
plaintext  = AES_GCM_decrypt(DEK, ciphertext)
blocks.caption: The envelope pattern in pseudocode

blocks.text: The payoff is operational, and it is significant:

items: Rotating the KEK means re-wrapping small DEKs, not re-encrypting terabytes of data.
The KEK can live somewhere the application cannot reach: the next lesson's HSM.
A leaked DEK exposes exactly one secret, because every secret has its own.
Deleting a wrapped DEK makes its ciphertext permanently unreadable: cryptographic erasure without touching the data.

blocks.text: AES-GCM is authenticated encryption: it provides confidentiality and integrity together, so tampering with ciphertext is detected rather than producing garbage plaintext.

Envelope encryption does not protect a secret from someone who can legitimately ask the system to decrypt it. It protects the data at rest. Authorization is a separate control; that is why access-control models get their own lesson.

quiz.question: Why does envelope encryption make key rotation cheap?
options: Rotating the KEK only requires re-wrapping small DEKs, not re-encrypting the data
The data is stored unencrypted
DEKs never need rotating
Rotation is deferred until the next read
quiz.explanation: The bulk data stays encrypted under its DEK. Only the small wrapped DEKs are re-encrypted under the new KEK, which is why rotation scales.

quiz.question: What is the effect of deleting a wrapped DEK while keeping the ciphertext?
options: The ciphertext is automatically deleted too
The DEK is regenerated on next read
Nothing, the KEK can still decrypt it
The ciphertext becomes permanently unreadable: cryptographic erasure
quiz.explanation: Without the DEK there is no way back to the plaintext. Destroying the key is an effective and instant way to erase data you cannot easily overwrite.

quiz.question: A single DEK is compromised. What is exposed?
options: Every secret under the same KEK
The KEK as well
Nothing: DEKs are not sensitive
Exactly one secret, because each secret has its own DEK
quiz.explanation: Per-secret DEKs limit the blast radius of a single key compromise to one value, which is the main security argument for the pattern.

title: Lab: build envelope encryption by hand
summary: Do the KEK and DEK dance yourself with openssl, then destroy a key and watch the data become unreadable.

blocks.text: The previous lesson described envelope encryption. Ten minutes with openssl makes it concrete, and nothing here needs an account, a network, or 1Claw. Everything happens in a scratch directory you delete afterwards.
You need openssl, which ships with macOS and every Linux distribution. Run `openssl version` to confirm.

steps.text: Make a scratch directory so nothing lands in a real project.
steps.code: mkdir -p /tmp/envlab && cd /tmp/envlab

steps.text: Generate the key encryption key. In production this lives inside an HSM and never comes out; here it is a file, which is exactly the weakness the HSM removes.
steps.code: openssl rand -hex 32 > kek.hex

steps.text: Generate a data encryption key for one secret. Every secret gets its own, which is what limits the blast radius of a single compromise.
steps.code: openssl rand -hex 32 > dek.hex

steps.text: Encrypt the secret under the DEK. Save the IV: it is not sensitive, but without it the ciphertext is undecryptable, which is a very common way to lose data.
steps.code:
printf 'sk-live-abc123' > secret.txt
openssl rand -hex 16 > iv.hex
openssl enc -aes-256-cbc \
  -K "$(cat dek.hex)" -iv "$(cat iv.hex)" \
  -in secret.txt -out secret.enc

steps.text: Wrap the DEK under the KEK. This is the envelope: the file you store next to the ciphertext is the encrypted key, never the key itself.
steps.code:
openssl rand -hex 16 > wiv.hex
openssl enc -aes-256-cbc \
  -K "$(cat kek.hex)" -iv "$(cat wiv.hex)" \
  -in dek.hex -out dek.wrapped

steps.text: Look at what a server would actually hold. There is no plaintext key anywhere in this list.
steps.code: ls -l secret.enc dek.wrapped iv.hex wiv.hex

steps.text: Read the secret back the way the vault does: unwrap the DEK with the KEK, then decrypt with the DEK.
steps.code:
openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc \
  -K "$(cat kek.hex)" -iv "$(cat wiv.hex)" \
  -in dek.wrapped -out dek.recovered

openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc \
  -K "$(cat dek.recovered)" -iv "$(cat iv.hex)" \
  -in secret.enc
# -> sk-live-abc123

steps.text: Before erasing anything, rotate the KEK. Take a fingerprint of the ciphertext, unwrap the DEK with the old KEK, generate a new KEK, and re-wrap the same DEK under it.
steps.code:
shasum -a 256 secret.enc

openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc \
  -K "$(cat kek.hex)" -iv "$(cat wiv.hex)" \
  -in dek.wrapped -out dek.plain

openssl rand -hex 32 > kek2.hex
openssl enc -aes-256-cbc \
  -K "$(cat kek2.hex)" -iv "$(cat wiv.hex)" \
  -in dek.plain -out dek.wrapped2

steps.text: Now fingerprint the ciphertext again, and compare the sizes of what rotation actually rewrote.
steps.code:
shasum -a 256 secret.enc
wc -c secret.enc dek.wrapped2

steps.text: Identical hash. You rotated the root of the hierarchy and the encrypted data was never opened, read or rewritten: rotation touched 80 bytes of wrapped key and left the ciphertext alone. On a real vault that is the difference between re-encrypting a small key and re-encrypting a database.
steps.code:
<hash>  secret.enc     (before)
<hash>  secret.enc     (after, identical)

      16 secret.enc
      80 dek.wrapped2
      96 total

steps.text: Now do cryptographic erasure. Delete only the wrapped DEK and try again.
steps.code:
rm dek.wrapped dek.recovered

openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc \
  -K "$(cat kek.hex)" -iv "$(cat wiv.hex)" \
  -in dek.wrapped -out dek.recovered
# -> Can't open "dek.wrapped" for reading, No such file or directory

steps.text: The ciphertext is untouched and permanently unreadable. Clean up.
steps.code: cd /tmp && rm -rf envlab

blocks.text: Three properties you just demonstrated rather than read about. The KEK never touched the secret, only the DEK. Rotating the KEK would mean re-encrypting one small wrapped key, not the data. And deleting a key erased the data instantly, without overwriting a single byte of it.

Real implementations use AES-GCM rather than CBC, because GCM authenticates as well as encrypts, so tampering is detected instead of producing garbage plaintext. CBC is used here only because it needs fewer flags to demonstrate.

You just held a KEK in a file, which is the thing the next lesson exists to fix. Everything above is correct and still weak, because the root of the hierarchy sat on disk where any process could read it.

quiz.question: You deleted the wrapped DEK but kept the ciphertext. Why is the data unrecoverable?
options: The IV was deleted along with it
The KEK can only decrypt data it encrypted directly
The ciphertext was overwritten when the DEK was deleted
There is no path back to the DEK, and only the DEK can decrypt the ciphertext
quiz.explanation: Cryptographic erasure works because the data is only reachable through the key. Destroying the small wrapped key is instant and complete, with no need to overwrite the data itself.

quiz.question: Why does each secret get its own DEK rather than sharing one?
options: It allows a shorter key length
It makes encryption faster
The KEK can only wrap one key at a time
A compromised DEK exposes exactly one secret
quiz.explanation: Per-secret DEKs bound the blast radius. One leaked DEK is one leaked secret, whereas a shared key would turn any single compromise into a full-store compromise.

quiz.question: The IV was stored in plaintext next to the ciphertext. Is that a problem?
options: No, and it can safely be discarded after encrypting
Yes, the IV must be kept as secret as the key
Yes, it lets an attacker recover the DEK
No, an IV is not secret, but losing it makes the ciphertext undecryptable
quiz.explanation: An IV needs to be unique, not confidential. It is stored alongside the ciphertext by design, but it is required for decryption, so losing it destroys the data as surely as losing the key.

title: Public-key cryptography and digital signatures
summary: Separate the key that proves identity from the key that verifies it, and see why signing is not encryption.

blocks.text: Symmetric encryption needs both parties to share a key. Public-key cryptography breaks that requirement with a mathematically linked pair: a private key you keep, and a public key you hand out freely.

items: Encrypt with the public key, decrypt with the private key; that gives confidentiality to the holder.
Sign with the private key, verify with the public key; that gives authenticity and integrity to everyone.

blocks.text: Signing is not encryption. A signature does not hide the message; it proves who produced it and that it has not changed. People conflate these constantly, and the confusion leads to real design errors.

A signature is computed over a hash of the message, not the message itself. That is why a signature is a fixed small size regardless of what it signs, and why the hash function's collision resistance matters as much as the signing algorithm.

items: secp256k1 (ECDSA): the curve used by Ethereum and Bitcoin.
Ed25519 (EdDSA): faster, with fewer implementation traps; used by Solana, XRP, Cardano, and SSH.
RSA: older and larger, still ubiquitous in enterprise and OIDC because everything can verify it.

blocks.text: This is why blind signing is dangerous. If you sign a 32-byte hash without seeing what produced it, you are vouching for a message you cannot read. It appears again in the agent threat model track.

Two properties follow that matter enormously later. Non-repudiation: a valid signature means the private key was used, so the holder cannot plausibly deny it. And verification needs no secret at all: anyone with the public key can check, which is what makes federated trust possible without shared credentials.

quiz.question: What does a digital signature provide that encryption does not?
options: A smaller message size
Protection against replay
Proof of who produced the message and that it is unchanged
Confidentiality of the message
quiz.explanation: Signatures give authenticity and integrity. They deliberately do not hide the message; encryption is the separate tool for confidentiality.

quiz.question: Why is a signature computed over a hash rather than the whole message?
options: Hashes are encrypted more securely
It makes verification require the private key
It keeps the signature a fixed small size regardless of message length
It prevents replay attacks
quiz.explanation: Signing a fixed-length digest keeps signatures small and fast. It also means the hash function's collision resistance is part of the security of the scheme.

quiz.question: Why is blind signing a 32-byte digest risky?
options: It uses a weaker curve
You vouch for a message you cannot read
Digests are easy to forge
It reveals the private key
quiz.explanation: If you cannot reconstruct what produced the hash, you have no idea what you authorized. This is the root of a whole class of wallet-drain attacks.

title: Lab: sign, verify, then tamper
summary: Generate an Ed25519 keypair, sign a message, verify it with the public key alone, and watch one changed character destroy the signature.

blocks.text: The previous lesson claimed that a signature proves authorship and detects modification, and that verification needs no secret. Three minutes of openssl turns all three claims into things you have seen.

steps.text: Make a scratch directory and generate an Ed25519 private key.
steps.code:
mkdir -p /tmp/siglab && cd /tmp/siglab
openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out private.pem

steps.text: Derive the public key. This is the half you hand out, and it cannot be used to sign.
steps.code:
openssl pkey -in private.pem -pubout -out public.pem
cat public.pem

steps.text: Write a message worth being careful about, and sign it with the private key.
steps.code:
printf 'transfer 10 ETH to 0xAlice' > msg.txt
openssl pkeyutl -sign -inkey private.pem -rawin -in msg.txt -out msg.sig
wc -c < msg.sig   # 64 bytes, regardless of message length

steps.text: Verify using only the public key. Note what you did not need: the private key, a shared secret, or a call to anyone.
steps.code:
openssl pkeyutl -verify -pubin -inkey public.pem -rawin -in msg.txt -sigfile msg.sig
# -> Signature Verified Successfully

steps.text: Now tamper. Change the recipient and check the original signature against it.
steps.code:
printf 'transfer 10 ETH to 0xMallory' > tampered.txt
openssl pkeyutl -verify -pubin -inkey public.pem -rawin -in tampered.txt -sigfile msg.sig
# -> Signature Verification Failure

steps.text: Confirm the message was never hidden. The signature protects it; it does not conceal it.
steps.code:
cat msg.txt
# -> transfer 10 ETH to 0xAlice

steps.text: One more check, and it is the one that matters later. Generate a second, unrelated keypair and verify the original signature against it.
steps.code:
openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out other.pem
openssl pkey -in other.pem -pubout -out other.pub

openssl pkeyutl -verify -pubin -inkey other.pub \
  -rawin -in msg.txt -sigfile msg.sig

steps.text: It fails, which is correct and is not the interesting part. The interesting part is what that implies.
steps.code: Signature Verification Failure

steps.text: Clean up.
steps.code: cd /tmp && rm -rf siglab

blocks.text: A signature carries no indication of which key produced it. Verification answers "was this signed by the key I am holding", and it can only answer that because you chose which key to check against. Choose the wrong one and a perfectly genuine signature is rejected; fail to pin down which one is correct and you will eventually accept a genuine signature from the wrong signer.

That is the whole problem the next lessons keep returning to. A JWT names its key in the kid header and its intended recipient in aud, and a verifier that checks the signature without checking those is asking the wrong question correctly.

The signature stayed 64 bytes whatever you signed, because signing operates on a fixed-length hash of the message rather than the message itself. That is also why the hash function's collision resistance is part of the security of the scheme and not a separate concern.

You verified with a public key and could not have signed with it. That asymmetry is what makes federated trust possible: a relying party validates 1Claw-issued tokens against published JWKS without holding any shared secret.
Now imagine signing msg.sig's contents without ever seeing msg.txt. That is blind signing, and it is why raw digest signing is gated behind a human-set flag in the Intents API.

quiz.question: The signature was 64 bytes for a short message. What would it be for a 4GB file?
options: Rejected as too large to sign
Still 64 bytes, because signing operates on a fixed-length hash
Split into multiple signatures
Proportional to the file size
quiz.explanation: The message is hashed to a fixed-length digest first, so signature size is constant. It is also why the hash function's collision resistance matters as much as the signing algorithm.

quiz.question: You verified the signature with public.pem. Could you have produced a signature with it?
options: Yes, public keys can both sign and verify
Only for messages under 64 bytes
No, signing requires the private key, which is what makes verification safe to delegate
Only with the original message present
quiz.explanation: The asymmetry is the whole point. Anyone can check, only the key holder can produce, which is what allows verification without sharing a secret.

quiz.question: After tampering, verification failed. What did that demonstrate?
options: Integrity: any modification is detectable by anyone holding the public key
The message is encrypted by the signature
The tampered file was corrupt
The private key had expired
quiz.explanation: Signing gives integrity and authenticity. It gives no confidentiality at all, which is why you could still cat the message in plaintext.

title: HSMs, KMS, and hardware roots of trust
summary: Learn what it means for a key to be non-exportable, and why that changes the shape of an attack.

blocks.text: Every scheme so far assumes some key must ultimately be protected. A hardware security module is the answer: a tamper-resistant device that generates keys internally and performs operations with them, without ever releasing the key material.
The critical property is non-exportability. You do not ask an HSM for the key. You send it data and ask it to sign or decrypt, and it returns the result.

This changes what an attacker gets. Compromise an application server holding a key file and they take the key: permanently, silently, and they can use it anywhere. Compromise a server that can call an HSM and they can use the key while they hold that access, but they cannot take it with them, and every use is logged.

items: Generation: the key is created inside the boundary and never exists outside it.
Use: sign, verify, wrap, unwrap are performed on the device.
Attestation: the device can prove a key was generated in hardware.
Audit: every operation is recorded, so use is observable even when authorized.

blocks.text: A KMS is the managed service wrapper around this: an API for creating keys, defining who may use them for what, and rotating them, with the private material staying inside a hardware boundary. Key versions matter: rotating creates a new version while old versions remain available for decrypting old data.

An HSM protects against key theft, not key misuse. If an attacker can call the API with valid credentials, the HSM will faithfully perform the operation. Non-exportability limits what they can steal, not what they can do while they have access.

Combine this with the previous lesson and the hierarchy appears: the KEK lives in the HSM and never leaves; DEKs are wrapped by it; the plaintext data is encrypted by the DEKs. The root of trust is hardware, and everything above it is derived.

quiz.question: What does non-exportability actually prevent?
options: Any unauthorized use of the key
The key from being rotated
Audit logs from being tampered with
An attacker taking the key material away for later or elsewhere
quiz.explanation: The key cannot leave the hardware boundary, so it cannot be exfiltrated. It does not stop an attacker with valid API access from using the key while they have that access.

quiz.question: Why keep old key versions after rotation?
options: To allow rollback of the rotation
Compliance forbids deletion
Data encrypted under previous versions still needs to be decryptable
Old versions are more secure
quiz.explanation: Rotation creates a new version for new operations, while old versions remain available so previously encrypted data stays readable.

quiz.question: In the envelope hierarchy, which key lives in the HSM?
options: The KEK
Both, equally
Neither: the HSM holds ciphertext
The DEK
quiz.explanation: The KEK is the long-lived root that never leaves hardware. DEKs are generated per secret and stored wrapped by it.

title: Authentication vs authorization: JWTs, OAuth2, and OIDC
summary: Separate who you are from what you may do, and read a token well enough to know what it actually proves.

blocks.text: Two questions that get conflated constantly. Authentication asks who are you. Authorization asks what may you do. A system can be certain of your identity and still correctly refuse you.
A JSON Web Token is a signed, base64-encoded set of claims. Signed, not encrypted: anyone holding it can read the payload. That single fact is the source of a lot of accidental disclosure.

blocks.code:
{
  "iss": "https://issuer.example.com",  // who minted this
  "sub": "agent_01H...",                // who it is about
  "aud": "https://api.example.com",     // who it is FOR
  "exp": 1767225600,                    // when it dies
  "iat": 1767224700,
  "scope": "secrets:read"               // what it permits
}
blocks.caption: A JWT payload. Readable by anyone holding the token: never put a secret in one.

blocks.text: Always validate iss, aud, and exp. A token that is cryptographically valid but was minted for a different audience is a confused-deputy attack waiting to happen, and it will pass a naive signature check.

items: OAuth2 is an authorization framework: it issues access tokens that say what a bearer may do.
OIDC is a thin identity layer on top of OAuth2; it adds an id_token that says who the user is.
A bearer token means exactly what it sounds like: whoever holds it can use it. There is no binding to the holder unless you add one.

blocks.text: Because bearer tokens are transferable, the main defence is time. A token that lives fifteen minutes is a far smaller prize than one that lives forever, and it makes the exchange pattern worth the complexity: hold a long-lived credential somewhere safe, exchange it for a short-lived token at the point of use.

JWKS, a published set of public keys, lets any party verify a token without holding a shared secret. Each key has a kid so the verifier knows which one to use, and keys can rotate without coordinating with every consumer.

quiz.question: Is the payload of a signed JWT confidential?
options: Only the claims marked private
Yes, the signature encrypts it
No: it is base64-encoded and readable by anyone holding the token
Yes, if the algorithm is RS256
quiz.explanation: Signing provides integrity and authenticity, not confidentiality. Anyone with the token can decode and read every claim, so secrets must never be placed in one.

quiz.question: Why must a verifier check the aud claim?
options: Without it the signature cannot be verified
aud identifies the signing key
aud determines the expiry
A token minted for another service may otherwise be replayed against yours
quiz.explanation: A cryptographically valid token issued for a different audience will pass a naive signature check. Validating aud is what stops it being replayed against your service.

quiz.question: What is the primary defence against a stolen bearer token?
options: Storing it in localStorage
Encrypting the token payload
Using a longer signing key
A short expiry, so the window of use is small
quiz.explanation: Bearer tokens are transferable by design. Since you cannot stop a thief holding one from using it, you limit how long it remains useful.

title: Lab: read a token, then replay it
summary: Decode a JWT with nothing but base64, then mint one for another service and watch a naive verifier accept it.

blocks.text: The previous lesson said a signed JWT is readable by anyone holding it. That is worth proving rather than believing, because the belief that a token is opaque is behind a lot of accidental disclosure.

steps.text: Save a token. This one is a realistic 1Claw agent JWT with a fake signature, so there is nothing sensitive here.
steps.code:
cat > /tmp/jwt.txt <<'EOF'
eyJhbGciOiJFZERTQSIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCIsImtpZCI6ImVkZHNhLXYzIn0.eyJpc3MiOiJodHRwczovL2FwaS4xY2xhdy5jbyIsInN1YiI6ImFnZW50XzAxSDhYSyIsImF1ZCI6Imh0dHBzOi8vYXBpLjFjbGF3LmNvIiwiZXhwIjoxNzY3MjI1NjAwLCJzY29wZSI6InNlY3JldHM6cmVhZCJ9.c2lnbmF0dXJlLWJ5dGVz
EOF

steps.text: Decode the payload. Note what you did not need: a key, a network call, or permission.
steps.code:
cut -d. -f2 /tmp/jwt.txt | python3 -c "
import sys, base64, json
s = sys.stdin.read().strip()
print(json.dumps(json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(s + '=' * (-len(s) % 4))), indent=2))
"

steps.text: You should see the claims in the clear.
steps.code:
{
  "iss": "https://api.1claw.co",
  "sub": "agent_01H8XK",
  "aud": "https://api.1claw.co",
  "exp": 1767225600,
  "scope": "secrets:read"
}

steps.text: Decode the header too. It names the algorithm and the key id the verifier should use from the JWKS.
steps.code:
cut -d. -f1 /tmp/jwt.txt | python3 -c "
import sys, base64, json
s = sys.stdin.read().strip()
print(json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(s + '=' * (-len(s) % 4))))
"

steps.text: Now the part that matters. Build two services that both trust the same issuer, and have one of them verify only the signature.
steps.code:
cat > /tmp/aud.py <<'EOF'
import hmac, hashlib, base64, json

KEY = b"issuer-signing-key"          # stands in for the issuer's key
b64   = lambda b: base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()
unb64 = lambda s: base64.urlsafe_b64decode(s + "=" * (-len(s) % 4))

def mint(payload):
    h = b64(json.dumps({"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}).encode())
    p = b64(json.dumps(payload).encode())
    sig = b64(hmac.new(KEY, f"{h}.{p}".encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest())
    return f"{h}.{p}.{sig}"

def signature_valid(tok):
    h, p, s = tok.split(".")
    return hmac.compare_digest(
        s, b64(hmac.new(KEY, f"{h}.{p}".encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest()))

claims = lambda tok: json.loads(unb64(tok.split(".")[1]))

# A token the billing service legitimately holds.
tok = mint({"iss": "https://api.1claw.co", "sub": "agent_01H8XK",
            "aud": "https://billing.example.com", "scope": "invoices:read"})
print("minted for:", claims(tok)["aud"])

print("\n=== deploy service, checking only the signature ===")
print("  ->", "ACCEPTED" if signature_valid(tok) else "REJECTED")

print("\n=== the same check, with the audience ===")
def verify(tok, me):
    if not signature_valid(tok):     return "REJECTED (bad signature)"
    if claims(tok).get("aud") != me: return f"REJECTED (aud is {claims(tok)['aud']})"
    return "ACCEPTED"
print("  deploy  ->", verify(tok, "https://deploy.example.com"))
print("  billing ->", verify(tok, "https://billing.example.com"))
EOF
python3 /tmp/aud.py

steps.text: A cryptographically valid token, issued to somebody else, accepted by a service it was never meant for.
steps.code:
minted for: https://billing.example.com

=== deploy service, checking only the signature ===
  -> ACCEPTED

=== the same check, with the audience ===
  deploy  -> REJECTED (aud is https://billing.example.com)
  billing -> ACCEPTED

steps.text: Clean up.
steps.code: rm /tmp/jwt.txt /tmp/aud.py

blocks.text: The signature proved the issuer and nothing else. Every customer of that issuer can mint a validly signed token, so a service that stops at signature verification will accept tokens minted for anybody. This is the confused deputy in its smallest form, and it is one missing line of code.

items: iss tells you who minted it. Check it, or you will accept tokens from any issuer whose key you happen to have.
aud tells you who it is for. Check it, or you accept tokens meant for someone else.
exp tells you when it dies. Check it, with a little clock skew tolerance, because short TTLs make tight expiry checks brittle.

blocks.text: Most JWT libraries verify the signature by default and leave the claim checks to you. A call that returns the decoded payload without throwing is not a call that has authorised anything.

This is exactly why 1Claw's federation tokens carry an audience and why an agent's federation_audiences allowlist is empty, meaning deny, until you fill it. The issuer constrains what may be requested; your service still has to check what it received.

You also could not alter the token. Editing any claim invalidates the signature, which is the split at the centre of the previous lesson: signing gives integrity and authenticity, never confidentiality.

quiz.question: What did decoding the payload require?
options: The signing key
The public key from the JWKS
The issuer's permission
Nothing but the token itself
quiz.explanation: A signed JWT is encoded, not encrypted. Anyone holding it reads every claim, which is why a secret must never be placed in one.

quiz.question: The deploy service verified the signature and accepted a token minted for billing. What was missing?
options: An expiry check
An audience check: the signature proves the issuer, not the intended recipient
A stronger algorithm
A fresher JWKS
quiz.explanation: Any customer of the same issuer can mint a validly signed token. Checking aud is what stops one being replayed against a service it was never issued for, and it is a single line.

quiz.question: Why does `base64 -d` often fail on a JWT segment?
options: The payload is encrypted
Segments are compressed first
Each segment uses a different encoding
JWTs use base64url with padding stripped, so it must be re-added
quiz.explanation: base64url swaps two characters and drops the trailing equals signs. Restoring the padding is what lets a standard decoder read it.

title: Lab: leak a secret with a stopwatch
summary: Measure a real side channel. Compare a token the obvious way, watch the clock reveal how much of it you guessed right, then fix it in one line.

blocks.text: Every lesson so far has treated a comparison as free. It is not. A comparison that stops at the first difference takes longer the more of the secret you already have, and that difference is measurable, which turns a token check into an oracle.

steps.text: Write the measurement. The naive comparison is the one people write by hand; compare_digest is the standard-library alternative.
You should see something close to this. The exact numbers vary by machine; the shape does not.
steps.code:
correct prefix        naive (ns)  compare_digest
 0 bytes                   191.3            39.8
 5 bytes                   302.6            40.1
10 bytes                   394.6            39.8
15 bytes                   489.6            39.8
20 bytes                   571.2            39.9

blocks.text: Read the naive column. It climbs steadily with the number of correct bytes, because the loop runs one iteration further before it can return. An attacker who can time your endpoint does not need to guess the whole token: they guess one byte at a time, keep whichever guess was slowest, and recover the secret in linear rather than exponential attempts.

items: A 20-byte token has 256^20 possible values, which is unguessable.
Guessed one byte at a time it is 20 x 256 attempts at worst, which is trivial.
The comparison, not the token, is what collapsed the search space.

blocks.text: compare_digest stays flat because it always inspects every byte, and combines the results, before returning. Constant time here means independent of the data, not fast.

Use a constant-time comparison for anything an attacker can supply and retry: API keys, session tokens, HMAC signatures, password hashes, TOTP codes. Python has hmac.compare_digest, Node has crypto.timingSafeEqual, Go has subtle.ConstantTimeCompare.

This is the first lesson in the track where the cryptography was flawless and the system leaked anyway. The key was strong, the token was random, and an ordinary equals sign gave it away. Most real breaks look like this rather than like broken maths.

quiz.question: Why does the naive comparison get slower as more of the guess is correct?
options: Longer strings take longer to hash
It returns at the first mismatch, so a longer correct prefix means more iterations
Python caches partial matches
The secret is re-read from memory each time
quiz.explanation: Early return is the leak. The running time is a function of how much of the secret the attacker already has, which is exactly the information they are trying to obtain.

quiz.question: What does an attacker gain from the timing difference?
options: They can recover the token one byte at a time, turning an exponential search into a linear one
They learn the token's length only
They can only detect that a token is wrong
Nothing without the private key
quiz.explanation: Guessing byte by byte reduces 256^20 possibilities to roughly 20 x 256 attempts. The search space collapses because each guess is scored independently.

quiz.question: What makes compare_digest constant time?
options: It adds random delay to mask the real time
It hashes both values first
It is implemented in C, so it is faster
It always examines every byte before returning, so the duration does not depend on the input
quiz.explanation: Constant time means independent of the data, not fast. Adding random delay is a common and unreliable substitute, because averaging over many samples recovers the signal.

title: Access control models and policy engines
summary: Compare RBAC, ABAC, and policy-as-code, and understand why deny-by-default is the only safe starting point.

blocks.text: Once identity is settled, something has to decide what that identity may do. Three models dominate, and they layer rather than compete.

items: ACL: a list attached to a resource saying who may touch it. Simple, and it sprawls badly.
RBAC: permissions attach to roles, identities get roles. Scales with people; struggles with context.
ABAC: decisions consider attributes of the principal, the resource, the action, and the environment. Expressive enough for 'only during business hours, from this network, on non-production data'.

blocks.text: Policy-as-code is the natural end point: rules live in a declarative language, are version-controlled, reviewed, and tested like any other code. Cedar and Rego are two widely used examples.

Deny-by-default is the single most important choice in this lesson. An allowlist fails closed: a rule you forgot means access is refused. A denylist fails open: a case you did not anticipate means access is granted. Only one of those failure modes is survivable.
Real engines need a conflict rule, because policies overlap. Two common designs:

items: Deny always wins: simple and predictable, but you cannot carve an exception out of a deny.
Explicit priority: each rule carries a number and the highest wins, which is more flexible and demands more care.

blocks.text: Know which model your system uses before you write a deny rule. Assuming deny always wins, in a system that resolves by priority, produces a rule that silently does nothing.

Finally, separate the decision from the enforcement. A policy decision point evaluates the rules; a policy enforcement point sits in the request path and applies the answer. Keeping them apart is what lets you test policy in isolation, and run it in shadow mode before it can break anything.

quiz.question: Why is deny-by-default safer than deny-by-exception?
options: A forgotten rule refuses access rather than granting it
It requires fewer policies
It is faster to evaluate
It logs more detail
quiz.explanation: Allowlists fail closed and denylists fail open. With deny-by-default the cost of an oversight is a support ticket, not a breach.

quiz.question: In an engine that resolves conflicts by priority, what happens to a deny rule with a lower priority than an overlapping allow?
options: The deny wins regardless
Both are ignored
The allow wins and the deny has no effect
The request errors
quiz.explanation: Under priority resolution, deny has no inherent advantage. A deny rule written on the assumption that 'deny always wins' can silently do nothing.

quiz.question: What is the point of separating the decision point from the enforcement point?
options: It removes the need for authentication
Policy can be tested and shadow-run independently of the request path
It allows denylists to be used safely
It improves latency
quiz.explanation: Separating them lets you evaluate policies against real or historical inputs without those decisions affecting live traffic, which is exactly what shadow mode does.

title: RBAC and why roles stop scaling
summary: Design roles properly, recognise role explosion before it happens, and understand why RBAC alone fails for agents.

blocks.text: Role-based access control is the model most developers meet first, and usually the one already in place wherever you work. Permissions attach to roles, roles attach to people, and nobody manages individual grants. It scales with headcount beautifully, and it is worth understanding exactly where it stops.

items: A permission is an action on a resource: read a secret, deploy a service, approve a payment.
A role is a named bundle of permissions: on-call engineer, billing admin.
An assignment binds a principal to a role, usually for as long as they hold a job.

blocks.text: The reason RBAC won is administrative rather than technical. When someone changes teams you change one assignment, not forty grants, and when an auditor asks who can approve payments you read one role rather than reconstructing it.

Role explosion is the characteristic failure, and it arrives the same way every time. A role nearly fits someone, so a variant is created. Then a variant of the variant. Within two years there are more roles than people, each held by one person, and the model has quietly degraded into per-user grants with extra indirection.

items: The warning sign is roles whose names contain a team, a person, or a project.
The measurement is the ratio of roles to principals. Approaching one to one means the model has stopped working.
The cause is almost always that context is being encoded into role names, because the model has nowhere else to put it.

blocks.text: That last point is what ABAC exists to fix. When the real rule is "an on-call engineer, during their shift, from a managed device", RBAC can only express it by making a role per combination. ABAC evaluates the attributes at request time and the roles stay stable.

For agents, RBAC breaks differently and more seriously. Roles model durable job functions, and an agent's justified access is narrow, short-lived and specific to a task. Giving an agent the deploy-bot role grants it whatever that role accumulates over time, from every future change made for reasons unrelated to it.

items: A human's access is stable for months; an agent's is often justified for minutes.
A human holds one role across many tasks; an agent should hold different access per task.
A human can be asked why they used a permission; an agent used it because its input said so.

blocks.text: Use roles for people and scoped, expiring policies for agents. Reusing a human role for an agent is convenient on the first day and is how an agent ends up with the union of everything that role ever needed.

The models compose rather than compete. Most working systems are RBAC for coarse organisational structure, ABAC conditions for context, and per-principal policies for the machine identities that do not fit either.

quiz.question: What is the clearest sign of role explosion?
options: Permissions are added to existing roles
Users hold more than one role
The ratio of roles to principals approaches one to one
Roles are being renamed frequently
quiz.explanation: One role per person means you have per-user grants wearing role names. The usual cause is context being encoded into role names because the model cannot express it otherwise.

quiz.question: Why is RBAC a poor fit for agents specifically?
options: Agents need more permissions than any role provides
Roles are too slow to evaluate per request
Roles model durable job functions, while an agent's justified access is narrow, short-lived and task-specific
Agents cannot be assigned roles technically
quiz.explanation: An agent given a human role inherits everything that role accumulates over time, for reasons unrelated to the agent. Scoped, expiring policies match how agent access is actually justified.

quiz.question: The rule is "an on-call engineer, during their shift, from a managed device". Why does RBAC struggle?
options: Roles cannot be time-limited at all
It only supports one role per user
It has nowhere to put context, so conditions become new roles
It cannot express negative permissions
quiz.explanation: RBAC binds permissions to a name, not to circumstances. Encoding shift and device state as roles is the mechanism by which role explosion happens; ABAC evaluates those attributes at request time instead.

title: Lab: build a policy engine and break it
summary: Implement deny-by-default with priorities in fifteen lines, then watch a deny rule silently do nothing.

blocks.text: The previous lessons said that deny-by-default fails closed, and that priority rather than effect resolves overlapping rules. Both are easy to nod along to and easy to get wrong under deadline, so build the engine and let it bite you.
Each step appends to the same script, so every run reprints the sections before it. The expected output shown under each step is the new part; scroll to the bottom of your terminal to find it.

steps.text: Write the engine. It is a matcher, a conflict rule, and a default, which is genuinely all a policy engine is at its core.
steps.code:
cat > /tmp/policy.py <<'EOF'
import fnmatch

POLICIES = [
    {"name": "broad-read", "path": "app/**",         "effect": "allow", "priority": 10},
    {"name": "no-billing", "path": "app/billing/**", "effect": "deny",  "priority": 5},
]

def decide(path, policies):
    matches = [p for p in policies
               if fnmatch.fnmatch(path, p["path"].replace("**", "*"))]
    if not matches:
        return "DENY", "no policy matched (deny-by-default)"
    winner = max(matches, key=lambda p: p["priority"])
    return winner["effect"].upper(), f'{winner["name"]} (priority {winner["priority"]})'

for path in ["app/search/key", "app/billing/stripe", "other/thing"]:
    verdict, why = decide(path, POLICIES)
    print(f"{path:24} {verdict:6} <- {why}")
EOF
python3 /tmp/policy.py

steps.text: Read the middle line carefully. The deny rule matched, and lost.
steps.code:
app/search/key           ALLOW  <- broad-read (priority 10)
app/billing/stripe       ALLOW  <- broad-read (priority 10)
other/thing              DENY   <- no policy matched (deny-by-default)

steps.text: Now raise the deny above the allow and run it again.
steps.code:
cat >> /tmp/policy.py <<'EOF'

print("\n--- raise the deny above the allow ---")
FIXED = [dict(p, priority=100) if p["name"] == "no-billing" else p
         for p in POLICIES]
for path in ["app/search/key", "app/billing/stripe"]:
    verdict, why = decide(path, FIXED)
    print(f"{path:24} {verdict:6} <- {why}")
EOF
python3 /tmp/policy.py

steps.text: Same rules, same paths, different outcome. The script re-runs both cases, so you get the before and after together.
steps.code:
app/search/key           ALLOW  <- broad-read (priority 10)
app/billing/stripe       ALLOW  <- broad-read (priority 10)
other/thing              DENY   <- no policy matched (deny-by-default)

--- raise the deny above the allow ---
app/search/key           ALLOW  <- broad-read (priority 10)
app/billing/stripe       DENY   <- no-billing (priority 100)

steps.text: Clean up.
steps.code: rm /tmp/policy.py

blocks.text: Two things happened, and the second is the one that ships to production.

items: The third path was denied by nothing at all. No rule mentioned other/thing, and the absence of a rule refused it. That is deny-by-default, and it is why an oversight becomes a support ticket rather than a breach.

The billing secret was allowed despite an explicit deny. The rule matched, it was correct, and it lost the comparison. Nothing errored, nothing warned, and a reviewer skimming the policy list sees a deny and assumes billing is protected.

blocks.text: This is the single most transferable bug in this course. Some engines resolve conflicts by deny-always-wins and some by priority, and a deny rule written against the wrong assumption is not a weak control, it is no control at all while looking like one.

Before you write a deny rule in any system, find out which model it uses. Then test the rule against a path it should refuse, because a silently inert policy looks identical to a working one in every list, diff and review.
The 1Claw policy engine resolves by priority, which is exactly the case this lab demonstrates. A deny needs a higher number than the allow it is carving into.

quiz.question: Why was other/thing denied when no rule mentioned it?
options: A hidden default-deny rule matched it
No policy matched, and the absence of a grant is a refusal
fnmatch rejects unknown prefixes
The path was malformed
quiz.explanation: Deny-by-default means access requires a positive grant. An allowlist fails closed, which is why a forgotten rule produces a support ticket rather than an exposure.

quiz.question: Why did the deny on app/billing/** have no effect in the first run?
options: It was defined after the allow in the list
The glob did not match the path
Deny rules are evaluated before allow rules
It matched but lost the priority comparison to the allow
quiz.explanation: The rule matched and was correct. Under priority resolution, deny has no inherent advantage, so a lower number means the rule is silently inert.

quiz.question: What should you do before writing a deny rule in an unfamiliar system?
options: Give it the lowest priority so it cannot cause an outage
Write it as a narrow allow instead
Place it first in the policy list
Establish whether conflicts resolve by priority or by deny-always-wins, then test it against a path it should refuse
quiz.explanation: The two models produce opposite outcomes for the same rules, and a rule written against the wrong assumption fails silently. Testing a path it should refuse is the only way to tell from the outside.

title: Threshold cryptography: Shamir and MPC
summary: Split trust so that no single party, including your own provider, ever holds a complete key.

blocks.text: An HSM removes the key from your application, but someone still operates the HSM. Threshold cryptography addresses the remaining question: what if you do not want any single party to hold the whole key?
Shamir's Secret Sharing splits a secret into n shares such that any t of them reconstruct it, and any t-1 reveal nothing at all. Not 'less information': mathematically nothing.

items: 2-of-2: both shares required. Maximum control, no fault tolerance.
2-of-3: any two of three. Survives losing one share, still tolerates one compromise.
The threshold t is the real security parameter; n only buys availability.

blocks.text: A t-1 set of Shamir shares leaks nothing. This is information-theoretic, not computational; it does not weaken as computers get faster.

Shamir has one weakness: reconstruction. To use the key, the shares come together somewhere, and at that instant the complete key exists in one place. Multi-party computation removes even that moment.

In threshold MPC the parties jointly produce a signature through a protocol, each using only its own share. The complete private key is never assembled anywhere, at any time. There is no instant to attack.

items: Split across providers: shares held by different HSM vendors, so no single vendor can act alone.
Client custody: one share held by you, so the provider mathematically cannot act without you.

blocks.text: Threshold schemes raise the operational cost of every signature and add real failure modes: lost shares, unavailable parties, protocol version drift. Use them where the trust assumption genuinely matters, not everywhere.

quiz.question: What do t-1 Shamir shares reveal about the secret?
options: Nothing at all: the guarantee is information-theoretic
Enough to brute force it
A partial reconstruction
The length of the secret
quiz.explanation: Below the threshold, the shares are consistent with every possible secret. The guarantee does not degrade with more computing power.

quiz.question: What does threshold MPC provide that Shamir sharing alone does not?
options: Protection against lost shares
Faster signing
Smaller shares
The complete key is never assembled, even momentarily
quiz.explanation: Shamir requires reconstruction to use the key, creating a moment where it exists whole. MPC produces the signature collaboratively so that moment never occurs.

quiz.question: In a 2-of-3 split, what does n = 3 buy you?
options: Availability: you can lose one share and still operate
Higher security than 2-of-2
Faster reconstruction
A lower threshold
quiz.explanation: The threshold t sets the security property; n provides redundancy so the loss of a single share is not fatal.

title: Lab: split a secret three ways
summary: Implement Shamir sharing in twenty lines, reconstruct from any two of three shares, then see for yourself that one share reveals nothing.

blocks.text: The previous lesson claimed that below the threshold a set of shares is consistent with every possible secret, and that this is information-theoretic rather than a matter of computational difficulty. That is a strong claim. Here it is, demonstrated.

steps.text: Write the implementation. Splitting hides the secret as the constant term of a random polynomial; recovery is Lagrange interpolation back to x = 0.
steps.code:
cat > /tmp/shamir.py <<'EOF'
import random
P = 2**127 - 1                    # prime field larger than any secret here

def split(secret, threshold, shares):
    coeffs = [secret] + [random.randrange(P) for _ in range(threshold - 1)]
    f = lambda x: sum(c * pow(x, i, P) for i, c in enumerate(coeffs)) % P
    return [(x, f(x)) for x in range(1, shares + 1)]

def recover(points):
    total = 0
    for i, (xi, yi) in enumerate(points):
        num = den = 1
        for j, (xj, _) in enumerate(points):
            if i != j:
                num = (num * -xj) % P
                den = (den * (xi - xj)) % P
        total = (total + yi * num * pow(den, -1, P)) % P
    return total

secret = int.from_bytes(b"launch-code-42", "big")
parts = split(secret, threshold=2, shares=3)
for x, y in parts:
    print(f"share {x}: {y}")

print("\nany two of three:")
for a, b in [(0,1), (0,2), (1,2)]:
    got = recover([parts[a], parts[b]])
    print(f"  {a+1}+{b+1} -> {got.to_bytes(14, 'big')}")

print("\none share alone is consistent with every possible secret:")
x, y = parts[0]
for guess in (0, 12345, secret):
    slope = ((y - guess) * pow(x, -1, P)) % P
    fits = (guess + slope * x) % P == y
    print(f"  secret could be {str(guess)[:20]:<20} -> share 1 still fits: {fits}")
EOF
python3 /tmp/shamir.py

steps.text: Every pair reconstructs the secret exactly.
steps.code:
any two of three:
  1+2 -> b'launch-code-42'
  1+3 -> b'launch-code-42'
  2+3 -> b'launch-code-42'

steps.text: And one share fits every candidate secret you try.
steps.code:
one share alone is consistent with every possible secret:
  secret could be 0                    -> share 1 still fits: True
  secret could be 12345                -> share 1 still fits: True
  secret could be 21982217121556893152 -> share 1 still fits: True

blocks.text: That last block is the whole property. With threshold two, one share is a single point, and exactly one line passes through that point for every possible value of f(0). The share does not narrow the secret down; it excludes nothing. Add a second point and the line is determined, which is why two shares recover it exactly.

This is why the guarantee does not weaken over time. It is not that reconstructing from one share is expensive, it is that the information is not present. No amount of computing changes that, which is what information-theoretic means.

Toy code, real maths. This implementation uses Python's random rather than a cryptographic source and does not authenticate shares, so a participant could submit a corrupted one and quietly poison the reconstruction. Production schemes handle both.

Now the operational half. You just held three shares in one process, which is precisely the moment threshold MPC removes: the shares came together, so the complete secret existed in one place. Everything you demonstrated about secrecy below the threshold was true and irrelevant during that instant.

quiz.question: With threshold two, why does a single share exclude no candidate secret?
options: The share is encrypted
Exactly one line passes through one point for every possible value of f(0)
Random noise is added to each share
The share is too short to be useful
quiz.explanation: One point does not determine a line. For any candidate secret there is a line through the share with that constant term, so the share is consistent with all of them.

quiz.question: Why does the guarantee not weaken as computers get faster?
options: The polynomial degree grows over time
The information is absent rather than merely hard to extract
The prime field is periodically increased
Shares are rotated automatically
quiz.explanation: Information-theoretic security is not a computational bound. There is nothing to compute because the missing information was never in the share.

quiz.question: What did holding all three shares in one process demonstrate about plain Shamir?
options: That reconstruction is fast
That shares must be stored together
That three shares are needed to recover
That using the secret requires assembling it somewhere, which is the moment MPC eliminates
quiz.explanation: Reconstruction creates an instant where the complete secret exists in one place. Threshold MPC produces the signature collaboratively so that moment never occurs.

title: Trusted Execution Environments
summary: Protect data while it is being used, not just at rest and in transit, and know what attestation does and does not prove.

blocks.text: Encryption at rest protects stored data. TLS protects data in transit. Both leave a gap: while a program runs, its data sits in memory in the clear, readable by anyone with sufficient privilege on that machine: including the operator.

A Trusted Execution Environment closes that gap with hardware. Memory is encrypted by the CPU, and code outside the enclave (the host OS, the hypervisor, the cloud provider's administrators) cannot read it.

items: AMD SEV-SNP and Intel TDX encrypt an entire virtual machine's memory.
Intel SGX isolates smaller enclaves within a process.
Remote attestation lets a third party verify what is running inside before trusting it with data.

blocks.text: Attestation is the part that makes this useful rather than merely comforting. The hardware signs a measurement of the code and configuration loaded into the enclave, and a remote party checks that signature against the expected value before releasing any secret to it.
Attestation proves which code is running. It does not prove that code is correct. A faithfully attested enclave running a flawed program is exactly as flawed: measured, verified, and wrong.

This is what makes a TEE a good place to put an inspection proxy. Traffic can be decrypted, examined, and re-encrypted inside the enclave, so sensitive content is inspected without the operator being able to observe it. That pattern reappears in the agent threat model track, where the traffic being inspected is prompts and completions.

TEEs have a real research literature of side-channel attacks: timing, cache, speculative execution. They raise the bar substantially rather than being unconditionally impenetrable. Treat them as a strong layer, not a guarantee.

quiz.question: Which gap does a TEE close that encryption at rest and TLS do not?
options: Data at rest on disk
Data in backups
Data in transit over the network
Data in use: while it sits in memory during execution
quiz.explanation: At-rest and in-transit encryption leave data readable in memory while a program runs. A TEE encrypts memory so even the host operator cannot read it.

quiz.question: What does remote attestation prove?
options: That the operator is trustworthy
That the data is encrypted at rest
That the code is free of bugs
Which code and configuration are running inside the enclave
quiz.explanation: Attestation is a hardware-signed measurement of what was loaded. It says nothing about whether that code is correct: a faithfully attested buggy program is still buggy.

quiz.question: Why is a TEE a good location for a traffic inspection proxy?
options: It guarantees the traffic is safe
It makes inspection faster
It removes the need for TLS
Traffic can be decrypted and inspected without the operator being able to observe it
quiz.explanation: The enclave can see plaintext to inspect it while the host operator cannot, which is what makes inspecting sensitive traffic acceptable.

title: Defense in depth and the weakest link
summary: Layer controls so that no single failure is fatal, and learn which classic principles actually earn their place.

blocks.text: Every control in this track can fail. Keys leak, policies are misconfigured, enclaves have side channels, and people approve things they should not. Defense in depth is the design response: assume any one layer fails, and arrange the others so that failure is survivable rather than total.
It is easy to say and easy to fake. Three layers that all depend on the same assumption are one layer wearing three hats.

items: Independent layers fail for different reasons. A network control and a cryptographic control are genuinely independent; two network controls from the same vendor largely are not.
Each layer should be individually meaningful. A control that only helps when another has already failed is a fallback, and worth having, but do not count it twice.
Layers must not create a false sense of coverage. The most common harm from a weak layer is the stronger control that never got built because someone believed the problem was handled.

blocks.text: Three older principles are worth knowing by name, because they are what the layering is made of.

items: Complete mediation. Every access is checked, every time, with no cached or implicit approval. A system that authorises once and then trusts a session indefinitely has a hole that widens with the session's lifetime.

Separation of duties. No single principal can complete a sensitive action alone. It is why a human approves what an agent proposes, and why the person who writes a policy should not be the only one who can approve widening it.

The weakest link. Attackers do not attack your strongest control; they go around it. Effort spent hardening something already strong is usually effort not spent on the part that will actually be attacked.

blocks.text: Complete mediation is the principle most often traded away for performance. Caching an authorization decision is exactly the optimisation that turns a revoked grant into one that stays live until the cache expires.

There is a real cost to layering, and pretending otherwise is how security teams lose credibility. Each layer adds latency, failure modes and operational burden, and a system with enough layers becomes one nobody fully understands. That is its own risk.

items: Prefer few strong, independent layers to many weak, correlated ones.
Every layer should have an owner who can explain what it stops and what it costs.
A layer nobody monitors is decorative; if its failure would be silent, it is not defending anything.

blocks.text: A useful test: for each control, name the specific failure of another control that it covers. If the answer is vague, you probably have redundancy rather than depth.

quiz.question: What distinguishes real defense in depth from layering that only appears deep?
options: The number of controls in the path
Whether the layers are all enabled by default
Whether each layer is from a different vendor
Whether the layers fail independently, for different reasons
quiz.explanation: Three controls sharing an assumption fail together. Independence is the property that makes a second layer worth its cost.

quiz.question: What does complete mediation require?
options: Every principal is authenticated at least once
Every access is checked every time, with no implicit or cached approval
All accesses are logged for later review
Access decisions are made by a central service
quiz.explanation: It is the principle most often traded away for performance, and caching an authorization decision is precisely what keeps a revoked grant alive until the cache expires.

quiz.question: What is the most common harm caused by a weak security layer?
options: The stronger control that never got built because someone believed the problem was handled
The false positives it generates
The latency it adds
The cost of licensing it
quiz.explanation: A weak layer that is honestly described as weak is fine. The damage comes from counting it as coverage, which stops the real control from being funded.

title: Threat modelling with STRIDE
summary: Use a checklist that has survived thirty years to find the threats you would otherwise have to be lucky to think of.

blocks.text: Every model in this course so far tells you what to do about a threat you already know about. Threat modelling is the step before that: enumerating threats systematically rather than relying on whoever is in the room having seen that failure before.
STRIDE is the oldest checklist still in wide use, and it earns its place by being memorable. Six categories, each the negation of a property you wanted.

items: Spoofing defeats authentication. Someone claims an identity that is not theirs.
Tampering defeats integrity. Data or code is modified in transit or at rest.
Repudiation defeats attribution. An actor denies having done something and you cannot prove otherwise.
Information disclosure defeats confidentiality. Data reaches someone it should not.
Denial of service defeats availability. A legitimate user cannot get the thing they need.
Elevation of privilege defeats authorization. Someone does something they were not permitted to do.

blocks.text: The method is mechanical, which is its strength. Draw the components and the flows between them, then walk each element against all six categories and ask what would go wrong. It surfaces the threats nobody would have volunteered, particularly repudiation and denial of service, which teams consistently skip.

steps.text: Take a concrete flow: a developer's CI job reads a secret and deploys.
steps.code:
CI runner  ->  1Claw API  ->  vault
     |
     +-------->  deploy target

steps.text: Walk it. Spoofing: could something other than your CI job present that credential? Tampering: could the deployed artifact be modified between build and deploy? Repudiation: if a bad deploy happens, can you prove which job did it?

Keep going. Information disclosure: does the secret reach the build log? Denial of service: what happens if the API is unavailable during a deploy? Elevation: can a job on a feature branch reach production paths?

blocks.text: Every one of those six questions maps to something earlier in this track: short-lived scoped credentials, signatures, audit logs, output masking, graceful degradation, and deny-by-default policy. The checklist is what makes you ask them all rather than the two you happened to think of.

STRIDE has real limits and it is worth naming them. It is oriented around a system diagram, so it finds threats to components you drew and says nothing about the ones you left out. It is weak on business-logic abuse, where every step is authorised and the sequence is the attack. And it predates agents entirely, which is why this course pairs it with the lethal trifecta and the OWASP agentic list rather than treating it as sufficient.

The failure mode of any threat-modelling exercise is producing a document. The output that matters is a short list of changes someone owns, and a shorter list of risks you decided to accept on purpose.

quiz.question: Which security property does repudiation defeat?
options: Attribution
Availability
Authorization
Confidentiality
quiz.explanation: Repudiation means an actor can deny an action and you cannot prove otherwise, which is why audit trails and signatures are the countermeasures.

quiz.question: What is the main practical value of walking a checklist like STRIDE?
options: It ranks threats by likelihood
It replaces the need for penetration testing
It produces documentation auditors require
It surfaces threat categories nobody in the room would have volunteered
quiz.explanation: Teams reliably think of disclosure and elevation, and reliably skip repudiation and denial of service. The mechanical walk is what makes the coverage even.

quiz.question: What is STRIDE weakest at?
options: Insider threats
Cryptographic weaknesses
Threats to components you did not draw, and business-logic abuse where each step is authorised
Network-level attacks
quiz.explanation: It is diagram-oriented, so its coverage is bounded by what you modelled, and a sequence of individually permitted actions does not trip any of the six categories.

title: Zero trust and least privilege
summary: Assemble the previous lessons into an architecture that assumes compromise rather than hoping to prevent it.

blocks.text: The perimeter model assumed a trusted inside and a hostile outside. It fails because it grants broad implicit trust to anything that gets in, and something always gets in.
Zero trust replaces location-based trust with per-request verification. Three commitments define it:

items: Never trust, always verify: every request is authenticated and authorized on its own merits, regardless of origin.
Assume breach: design so that a compromised component yields as little as possible.
Least privilege: every principal gets the narrowest grant that lets it do its job, for the shortest time.

blocks.text: Least privilege has three dimensions, and it is easy to remember only the first:

items: Scope: which resources, expressed as narrowly as the system allows.
Permission: read versus write; most principals need far less write access than they are given.
Time: how long the grant lasts. A permanent grant is a standing invitation.

blocks.text: Blast radius is the question to keep asking. Not 'can this be compromised' (assume it can) but 'what exactly does the attacker get when it is'. If the honest answer is 'everything', the design is wrong regardless of how good the controls are.

Everything in this track composes into one shape. Identity is established with signed, short-lived, audience-bound tokens. Authorization is decided by a deny-by-default policy engine, separately from enforcement. Key material is non-exportable in hardware, optionally split so no single party holds it. Sensitive processing happens inside an attested enclave. Every decision is logged for attribution.

That architecture was designed for services and humans. The next track examines what happens when the principal is a language model that can be talked into things, and which of these assumptions survive contact with that.

quiz.question: Why does the perimeter model fail?
options: It grants broad implicit trust to anything inside the boundary
It requires too many credentials
Firewalls are unreliable
It is too slow to evaluate
quiz.explanation: Once an attacker is inside, a perimeter model has little left to stop them. Zero trust removes the implicit trust that location previously conferred.

quiz.question: Which dimension of least privilege is most often overlooked?
options: Time: grants that never expire
Identity
Permission
Scope
quiz.explanation: Scope and permission get attention; duration is routinely ignored. A credential with no expiry converts a single leak into indefinite access.

quiz.question: What does 'assume breach' change about how you design?
options: You optimise for limiting what a compromise yields, not only for preventing it
You log less to reduce exposure
You stop investing in prevention
You require more passwords
quiz.explanation: Prevention still matters, but the design goal becomes minimising blast radius, because the probability of some compromise over time approaches certainty.
